questions.question: A science class tests a chemical called phenylthiocarbamide (PTC). Each student rests a paper strip soaked in it on the tongue. About three students in four taste something bitter, while the rest taste nothing at all. What causes the difference between them?
choices: The genes each student inherited
The part of the tongue the strip touched
How long each student held the strip
What each student ate for breakfast
questions.context: Whether a person tastes PTC depends on a gene called TAS2R38, passed down from parents, and about one person in four tastes no bitterness at all. Taste buds all over the tongue can sense bitterness; the old map of separate taste zones is a myth.
questions.grade_note: 6th-grade work on variation shows that members of one species differ in hidden ways as well as visible ones, and the PTC strip is the standard classroom test of an inherited one.

questions.question: A gardener's hydrangea bush has blue flowers. She grows a new plant from a cutting of it and gives it to a friend across town, where it blooms pink. What most likely changed the colour?
questions.answer: The soil in the friend's garden
choices: The soil in the friend's garden
A change in the cutting's genes
Pollen from the friend's other flowers
A hidden pink trait showing up in the cutting
questions.context: A cutting grows into a plant with exactly the same genes as the bush it came from, so neither a new gene nor a hidden trait can explain the change; the surroundings must. A bigleaf hydrangea blooms blue in acid soil, where its roots can take up aluminium, and pink in alkaline soil, where they cannot.
questions.grade_note: Telling inherited variation from variation caused by the surroundings is part of 6th-grade work on variation, and the hydrangea's soil colours are a well-known case of the second kind.

questions.question: Green and brown beetles of one species live on brown soil. Birds spot the green ones more easily and eat more of them. Generation after generation, a larger share of the beetles is brown. Why does the brown share keep growing?
questions.answer: More brown ones live to pass their colour on
choices: More brown ones live to pass their colour on
Green beetles turn brown to hide from the birds
Green beetles have brown young to keep them safe
The brown soil slowly stains the green beetles
questions.context: Fewer brown beetles are eaten, so more of them live long enough to breed, and their young are brown like them because colour is inherited. No beetle changes colour to suit the soil, and parents cannot give their young a colour because the young need it.
questions.grade_note: That members with a helpful variation survive and have young more often, so the variation becomes more common, is the heart of TEKS 6.13C, and the green and brown beetles are a standard teaching model for it.

questions.question: Biologists had just finished measuring the small lizards on two islands when two hurricanes struck in 2017. Returning weeks later, they found that the lizards still alive had bigger toe pads, on average, than the lizards there before the storms. What best explains the difference?
questions.answer: Lizards with bigger pads held on and lived
choices: Lizards with bigger pads held on and lived
The biggest, strongest lizards were the ones that lived
Clinging in the wind stretched each lizard's pads
The lizards grew bigger pads to grip the branches
questions.context: Most likely, the storms changed no lizard's feet: lizards that already had bigger toe pads could cling on better in the wind, and the survivors were smaller on average, so the biggest did not do best. The biologists called this the best explanation, though they could not rule out others, such as lizards blown in from another island. About a year and a half later, young lizards hatched since the storms had toe pads as big as the survivors'.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 6.13C asks how a variation can help survival when the environment changes; a hurricane is such a change, and this study is a widely reported real case.

questions.question: Seed-eating birds of one species on a small island have beaks that range from thin to thick. A long drought leaves only big, hard seeds, and the thick-beaked birds do best. Then years of heavy rain cover the island in plants with small, soft seeds. Which birds now raise the most young?
choices: The thin-beaked birds
The thick-beaked birds
The medium-beaked birds
Thick- and thin-beaked birds alike
questions.context: A thick beak cracks big, hard seeds, but a thinner beak eats small seeds more efficiently, so after the rains the thin-beaked birds grew faster and had more young. Biologists saw this among finches on a Galápagos island: a drought in 1977 favoured big beaks, and after heavy rains in 1982 and 1983 brought a flush of small seeds, the average beak shrank again within a few years. A variation that helps in one setting can hurt in another.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 6.13C asks how one variation can be an advantage or a disadvantage as conditions change, and thick and thin finch beaks are the example its teaching materials give.

questions.question: Swallows build mud nests under road bridges, and passing cars kill some of them. Biologists who picked up the dead birds for thirty years found that the dead had longer wings, on average, than the living. Over those years, what has happened to the swallows' wings?
questions.answer: On average, they have grown shorter
choices: On average, they have grown shorter
On average, they have grown longer
They have stayed the same length
Each bird's wings shrink as it gets older
questions.context: A shorter wing lets a swallow fly up and turn away from a car more quickly, so short-winged birds were killed less often and more of them lived to raise young. Over the thirty years the swallows' wings grew shorter on average and far fewer died on the road, though the biologists say other causes may play a part.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 6.13C asks how a variation can help or hurt as the environment changes, and a road full of traffic is a human-made change of that kind.

questions.question: A fungus has been killing ash trees across Europe, and in some woods most of them have died of the disease, called ash dieback. A few ash trees stay healthy beside their dying neighbours. Why might the ash survive as a species?
questions.answer: Seedlings of the healthy trees can inherit resistance
choices: Seedlings of the healthy trees can inherit resistance
Sick trees can catch resistance from the healthy ones
Dying trees will grow resistance before they die
Young trees are too small for the fungus to harm
questions.context: Some ash trees inherit a resistance to the fungus, and they can pass it to their seedlings; in one English wood, scientists found the new generation already more resistant, on average, than the old trees around it. Resistance does not spread from tree to tree like a cold, and young ash trees without it die fastest of all.
questions.grade_note: That variation within a population lets a species survive a change such as a new disease is the main idea of TEKS 6.13C.

questions.question: The Gros Michel was once the main banana shipped to Europe and North America. In the 1950s Panama disease, caused by a fungus, swept through its plantations in Central America and wiped out huge stretches of them. Why could one disease destroy so many?
questions.answer: Every plant was a copy of the same plant
choices: Every plant was a copy of the same plant
Insects spread the fungus from flower to flower
The fungus killed each plant in a few days
The disease was new and never seen before
questions.context: Bananas are grown from shoots of older plants, not from seeds, so every Gros Michel was a copy with the same genes and the same weakness. The disease was not new, and it works slowly: the fungus lives in the soil, creeps in through the roots and takes months to kill a plant. Growers switched to the Cavendish, which resisted that fungus, but every Cavendish is a copy too, and a new strain of the fungus now threatens it.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 6.13C asks how variation helps a population survive a change, and a crop with no variation at all, wiped out by one disease, shows the other side of that idea.

7f773b129c.why: Judge (medium, grade): with soil and sunlight both offered, choosing between them turned on hydrangea chemistry, not on the 6th-grade fact. 'Sunlight in the friend's garden' is replaced by an inherited confusion, a hidden trait showing up (wrong: a cutting has the bush's genes exactly, F11), so the science decides: a cutting is a copy, so the change came from the surroundings. Stem and key unchanged; the context now says why both inherited choices fail.

6544f4dac6.why: Fact-check error: the young lizards were surveyed 18 months after the first post-storm survey, not 'a year later' (Donihue et al. 2020, F26). Fact-check (uncertain) and judge (low): the context stated the grip story and 'the storms changed no lizard's feet' more firmly than the authors, who called it the best explanation and could not rule out lizards blown in from elsewhere; now hedged as they did. Natural selection is still not named. Stem, key and choices unchanged.

ee011a045a.why: Judge (medium, clarity): 'Which birds now do best?' let 'thick- and thin-beaked birds alike' be defended, since food was plentiful for all while the rains lasted. The question now asks which birds raise the most young, and the sources say the small-beaked finches had more offspring in the wet years (F28), so 'alike' is wrong as asked. Key and choices unchanged.

374bbe2a26.why: Fact-check error and judge (medium, fact): the stem called the fungus 'Panama disease'; Panama disease is the disease, caused by a fungus (F27). Judge (medium, tell): all three wrong choices were absolutes ('any fungus', 'every kind of plant', 'a single day') and one was silly. New wrong choices, none absolute and each truly wrong: insects carrying it between flowers (it lives in the soil and enters by the roots), death in a few days (it takes six to twelve months), and a brand-new disease (it had been known since 1874 and in Panama by 1890, F27). 'In the soil' is left out of the stem so it does not strike the insect choice; the context says it. Key unchanged.

dropped.question: Biologists count two animals as one species when they can mate and have young that grow up to have young of their own. By that test, which pair of animals belongs to a single species?
dropped.why: Judge (high, tell): everyday knowledge answers it, since every child knows a Chihuahua and a Great Dane are both dogs and that mixed breeds have puppies; and (medium, grade) the breeding test for a species is T3 classification and T5 speciation, with dog breeds the T3 artificial-selection unit's example. The judge's re-key to the term 'variations' would bring a new tell (the stem's 'differences' is the everyday meaning of the key, against three technical words), so the question is dropped rather than warped.

dropped.question: A gardener grows a kind of bean whose plants all carry the same genes. Some of her beans come out bigger than others, because they grew where the soil and sunlight were best. She sows only the biggest beans. How big will the beans of the new plants be?
dropped.why: Judge (high, drop) and the lead: same fact as the T3 pilot mendels-peas-and-inherited-traits (the blacksmith's strength gained in life is not inherited), also echoed by born-knowing-or-learned and adaptations-built-for-a-place at T1. No rewrite keeps the fact without the clash.
